description: Police statistics, the Crime Survey and victim surveys. Crime patterns and the dark figure of unreported offending.
content_html:
What Do We Actually Know About Crime?

Before sociologists can analyse crime, they must grapple with a fundamental methodological question: how is crime measured, and how reliable are those measurements? Different sources of crime data paint different pictures, and sociological perspectives disagree about what official statistics reveal, conceal and distort. This lesson examines the main sources of crime data, the patterns they reveal and their significant limitations.

Key Fact

The three main sources of crime data in England and Wales are: (1) police-recorded crime, (2) the Crime Survey for England and Wales (a large-scale victim survey), and (3) self-report studies. Each source captures different dimensions of crime and each has distinct strengths and limitations.

Police-Recorded Crime

Police-recorded crime refers to incidents that are reported to the police and recorded as crimes in their official statistics, published by the Home Office. This source has the longest historical run of data and allows analysis of trends over decades.

However, police-recorded crime has well-documented limitations. First, it only captures crimes that are reported to the police by victims or witnesses. Many crimes — particularly domestic violence, sexual offences, many thefts and hate crimes — are never reported. Second, even among reported crimes, the police have discretion about whether to record an incident as a crime: policing priorities, officer judgements and administrative recording practices all influence what enters the official figures. Third, changes in recording practices over time make comparisons difficult — a rise in recorded sexual offences, for example, may reflect increased willingness to report rather than increased incidence.

From a Marxist perspective, police-recorded statistics reflect the priorities and interests of those with power to define and enforce the law. Crimes committed by the powerful (corporate fraud, tax evasion, health and safety offences) receive less police attention and thus less recording, while street crime committed by the poorest groups is disproportionately pursued. The official statistics therefore tell us as much about policing choices as about crime.

The Crime Survey for England and Wales

The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW) was established in 1982 and asks a large representative sample of households in England and Wales about crimes they have experienced in the previous year, regardless of whether those crimes were reported to the police. By surveying victims directly, it provides a measure of crime that is independent of police recording decisions.

The CSEW consistently records higher crime levels than police-recorded figures because it captures many incidents that go unreported. It is therefore regarded by sociologists as a more comprehensive measure of crime experienced by the population. It also provides consistent data over time unaffected by changes in police recording practices.

The CSEW has its own limitations, however. It relies on self-report by respondents, who may misremember events, under-report sensitive offences (domestic abuse, sexual violence) out of shame or fear, or fail to recognise that an experience constituted a crime. It also excludes crimes against commercial premises, murder (where there is no living victim to survey), and crimes experienced by those living in institutions such as prisons or care homes. Crimes without a direct personal victim — such as drug possession or fraud against organisations — are also outside its scope.

Police-recorded crime: based on reports to the police; affected by policing priorities and recording decisions; shows long-term historical trends; captures crimes against businesses and public property; sensitive to changes in police practice.

Crime Survey for England and Wales: based on victim self-report; independent of policing decisions; more consistent over time; captures unreported crime; excludes murder, victimless crimes, crimes against organisations and under-reporting of sensitive offences.

When the two measures diverge (as they often do), sociologists ask which factors explain the gap. A rise in police-recorded crime during a period of stable CSEW figures, for example, is more likely to reflect improved recording practices than a real rise in offending.

Self-Report Studies

Self-report studies ask individuals to disclose crimes they have committed, often anonymously, providing a third source of data that challenges official crime statistics. Self-report studies have consistently shown that offending is far more widespread across social classes and ethnic groups than official statistics suggest — middle-class and white individuals commit offences at rates much closer to working-class and Black individuals than police-recorded crime implies. This finding supports the interactionist argument that official statistics reflect selective policing and prosecution rather than actual offending behaviour.

Self-report studies have their own limitations: respondents may under-report serious crimes (rape, grievous bodily harm) while over-reporting minor offences; they rely on accurate recall; and they cannot capture offences the respondent does not recognise as crimes or is unwilling to disclose even anonymously.

The Dark Figure of Crime

The dark figure of crime refers to the substantial gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount that appears in official statistics. This gap exists for two main reasons: crimes are not reported to the police, and crimes that are reported are not always recorded.

Key Fact

Victims may not report crime because: they consider it too trivial; they fear they will not be believed; they are intimidated by the offender; they feel embarrassed or ashamed; they distrust the police; or they resolve the matter informally. Police may not record a reported crime if they judge it insufficiently serious, if the victim withdraws the complaint, or if recording practices are inconsistent.

The dark figure is not evenly distributed across all crime types. Domestic violence and sexual offences have particularly large dark figures because of shame, fear of retaliation and the intimate relationship between victim and perpetrator. Fraud and cybercrime are significantly under-recorded because victims often do not recognise they have been defrauded, report to a bank rather than the police, or assume the police will not act. Minor property crime may go unreported simply because victims feel it is not worth the effort of reporting.

A very common error in sociology exams is to cite official crime statistics as if they were objective facts about the true level of crime in society. The spec is explicit that official statistics have both strengths and weaknesses and that sociological perspectives differ on their usefulness. The dark figure concept is the spec’s core illustration of why official statistics under-represent crime. Always evaluate statistics by asking: what is the source? Who is likely to be missing from this data? What policing or reporting decisions might affect these figures?

Sociological Perspectives on Crime Data

Sociological perspectives disagree about the value and meaning of official crime statistics. Functionalists broadly accept official statistics as a useful measure of crime trends, arguing that they allow governments to monitor social order and direct policing resources. Functionalists treat crime data as a reasonable approximation to reality, while acknowledging recording limitations.

Marxists are far more sceptical. They argue that crime statistics are socially constructed in the interests of the ruling class. The law itself is made by and for the bourgeoisie; enforcement focuses on working-class crime; and the statistics therefore reflect class power rather than objective harm. Official data systematically conceals corporate and white-collar crime while inflating working-class street crime.

Feminist perspectives point out that crime statistics consistently under-represent crimes against women, particularly domestic violence and sexual assault. Patriarchal norms discourage women from reporting these crimes; police response has historically been inadequate; and victim-blaming attitudes in courts further reduce the likelihood of prosecution. Feminists argue that the dark figure of gendered violence is particularly large and that official statistics should always be read critically in this light.

Interactionists argue that crime statistics measure policing activity rather than criminal behaviour. Because the police have discretion about whom to stop, search, arrest and charge, the statistics reflect which groups have been labelled as criminal rather than which groups actually offend more. Self-report studies, which show offending rates that are more evenly spread across social groups, support this critical reading of official data.
exam_tip_html: When answering a question about crime statistics, whether short or extended, always distinguish between police-recorded crime and the Crime Survey for England and Wales. Students who write “official statistics show that...” without specifying which source are leaving easy marks on the table. For the 12-mark Discuss question on crime data, the Mastering tier requires you to present at least two contrasting perspectives (for example, functionalist acceptance of official statistics as broadly useful versus Marxist critique of their class bias) and to reach a supported judgement. A strong conclusion might acknowledge that official statistics have genuine utility for identifying trends while also reflecting policing priorities that reproduce social inequality — that both points are true simultaneously is what “how far” questions invite you to argue.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three main sources of crime data are police-recorded crime, the Crime Survey for England and Wales (a victim survey), and self-report studies. Each captures different dimensions of crime and each has distinct strengths and limitations.
  • The dark figure of crime is the gap between actual crime and officially recorded crime. It exists because many crimes are never reported to the police, and because not all reported crimes are recorded. The dark figure is particularly large for domestic violence, sexual offences and fraud.
  • Sociological perspectives differ on the value of crime statistics: functionalists broadly accept them as useful trend data; Marxists argue they reflect class power and conceal corporate crime; feminists highlight the under-recording of crimes against women; interactionists argue they measure policing activity rather than offending behaviour.

practice_questions.text:
Which source of crime data asks members of the public about crimes they have experienced as victims, whether or not they reported them to the police?
A) Police-recorded crime statistics
B) The Crime Survey for England and Wales
C) Court conviction records
D) Prison population data
practice_questions.marks: B) The Crime Survey for England and Wales [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'the dark figure of crime'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that it refers to crime that does not appear in official statistics; 1 mark for specifying that this is because crimes are not reported to the police or not recorded by them. Example: 'The dark figure of crime is the gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount that is officially recorded, caused by victims not reporting incidents to the police and by the police not recording all reported crimes.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one reason why a victim might not report a crime to the police.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant reason (e.g. fear of not being believed; intimidation by the offender; shame or embarrassment; distrust of the police; considering it too trivial). Up to 2 marks for a developed description with sociological reasoning. Example: 'Victims of domestic violence may not report the crime because they fear or are financially dependent on the perpetrator (1). Feminist sociologists argue that patriarchal norms also discourage women from reporting sexual and domestic violence because of shame and the fear of victim-blaming responses from police and courts, resulting in a particularly large dark figure for these crimes (2 marks for a developed sociological point).'

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Crime Survey for England and Wales differs from police-recorded crime as a source of data.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Likely content: The CSEW is a large-scale victim survey that asks households directly about crimes they have experienced (1), whereas police-recorded crime is based on incidents reported to and recorded by the police (1). The CSEW therefore captures many crimes that are never reported to the police, producing higher estimates of crime levels (1). Because the CSEW is independent of policing decisions, it is less affected by changes in recording practices, making it a more consistent basis for long-term trend analysis (1).

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one limitation of self-report studies as a source of data on crime.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (e.g. respondents may under-report serious crimes; they may over-report minor ones; they rely on accurate recall; not everyone recognises their behaviour as criminal). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: 'Self-report studies rely on respondents honestly disclosing their own offending (1). Even when anonymity is guaranteed, participants may under-report serious offences such as sexual violence or serious assault because of shame or fear of consequences, meaning the most harmful crimes remain undercounted even in this source (2 marks for a developed, sociologically grounded point).'

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that official crime statistics are a reliable and useful measure of the true extent of crime in society. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering — Full range of relevant arguments for and against. For the statement: functionalist perspective accepts official statistics as useful indicators of crime trends, allowing governments to allocate policing resources and identify rising or falling crime; police-recorded crime offers the longest historical run of data; CSEW provides a consistently collected victim survey. Against the statement: the dark figure of crime demonstrates that official statistics systematically under-represent crime because many crimes are never reported or recorded; Marxist critique that the law and policing priorities protect ruling-class interests, concealing corporate and white-collar crime while inflating working-class crime; feminist critique that crimes against women (domestic violence, sexual assault) have a particularly large dark figure due to patriarchal norms; interactionist argument that statistics measure policing activity (who is labelled and prosecuted) rather than actual offending (self-report studies show offending is more evenly spread across groups). A clear, supported judgement weighing these critiques. Secure — Most relevant arguments, both sides, named perspectives. Judgement present if development uneven. Developing — Mostly one-sided or underdeveloped. Emerging — Basic descriptive points, little sociological reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes the 'dark figure of crime'?
options: The number of crimes committed at night
The gap between actual crime and officially recorded crime
Data on crimes that are solved by the police

flashcard_questions.q: What is the dark figure of crime?
flashcard_questions.a: The gap between actual crime and officially recorded crime, caused by non-reporting and non-recording.
Crime figures compiled from incidents reported to and recorded by the police, published by the Home Office.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Crime Survey for England and Wales?
flashcard_questions.a: A large-scale victim survey asking households about crimes they have experienced, whether or not reported to police.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Crime Survey for England and Wales established?
What are self-report studies in the context of crime research?
flashcard_questions.a: Research in which participants disclose their own offending behaviour, often anonymously, to reveal crime beyond official records.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do self-report studies challenge official crime statistics on class and ethnicity?
flashcard_questions.a: Because they show offending is more evenly spread across groups than police records suggest, supporting labelling theory.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two reasons why a victim might not report a crime.
flashcard_questions.a: Fear of not being believed; intimidation by the offender; shame; distrust of police; considering it too trivial.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Marxists argue that official crime statistics are unreliable?
flashcard_questions.a: Because policing priorities protect ruling-class interests, concealing corporate crime while inflating working-class crime.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do feminists argue that official statistics under-represent crimes against women?
flashcard_questions.a: Patriarchal norms, shame and inadequate police responses discourage women from reporting domestic and sexual violence.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do functionalists broadly accept official crime statistics as useful?
flashcard_questions.a: They treat them as reliable enough to identify trends and inform policing resource allocation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is domestic violence thought to have a particularly large dark figure?
flashcard_questions.a: Because victims fear the perpetrator, may depend on them financially, and face shame and victim-blaming responses.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one limitation of the Crime Survey for England and Wales?
flashcard_questions.a: It excludes murder, crimes against organisations, and relies on victims accurately recalling and recognising their experiences.

glossary_terms.definition: The gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount that is officially recorded, caused by non-reporting and non-recording of crimes.
Crime figures compiled from incidents recorded by the police, published by the Home Office as a measure of crime trends.

glossary_terms.term: Crime Survey for England and Wales
glossary_terms.definition: A large-scale social survey conducted by the Office for National Statistics, asking a sample of households about their experiences of crime as victims.
Research in which participants are asked to disclose their own offending behaviour, often anonymously, to provide a picture of crime beyond what official statistics record.
A survey that asks members of the public about crimes they have experienced as victims, regardless of whether those crimes were reported to the police.
Data collected and published by government agencies or departments, such as crime figures recorded by the police.
When a victim or witness of a crime chooses not to report the incident to the police.
